Montezuma II. The ninth Aztec emperor ruled from 1502 to 1520, presiding over a civilization at the height of its power until Spanish conquistadors arrived and everything collapsed. He inherited an empire of millions centered in Tenochtitlan, one of the world's largest cities. But when Hernán Cortés and his Spanish forces arrived, Montezuma made a fateful choice. He received them with hospitality rather than immediate military opposition, possibly viewing them as divine envoys. This hesitation became a catastrophic miscalculation once Spanish intentions became clear. As conflicts escalated, Montezuma suffered from profound indecision and allowed the Spanish to consolidate power and form alliances with tributary peoples who resented Aztec rule. Most damaging of all, he allowed himself to be taken captive by Cortés and held as a hostage to control the Aztec state itself. This unprecedented humiliation undermined his authority and religious prestige beyond recovery. He died in 1520 during the Spanish siege of Tenochtitlan, either from Spanish violence or wounds inflicted by his own people, disgusted by his perceived betrayal and weakness. The Spanish conquest was accelerated not by Spanish military might alone but by devastating smallpox epidemics that killed far more Aztecs than combat, wiping out much of the empire's population and military capacity within months. Modern indigenous scholarship reassesses his legacy as a statesman facing impossible choices rather than a simple fool, complicating the European narrative of inevitable conquest. He shared a father with various other Aztec rulers and his empire would be succeeded by Spanish colonial rule.
